Written by the Śramaṇa Yijing upon his return from the Western Regions to the Southern Sea.
Regarding the account composed by Li Foshi, sent from afar along with the map of Nālandā Monastery: observe that since ancient times,

Yet, the supreme path is fraught with many difficulties, and the place of the jewels is far distant.

In the vast and surging whale-waves, giant fish rise with waves that flood the heavens;
he strides alone beyond the Iron Gate,

It may be said that such deliberation exhausts the spirit and such anxiety and toil displace the natural countenance,

As for Dharma Master Xuanzhao of Taizhou—Dharma Master Xuanzhao, a śramaṇa—is as follows:
He was a native of Xianzhang in Taizhou.
His Sanskrit name was Paṅkasa-mati, which in the language of Tang means "Illuminating Wisdom. His ancestors and parents had held hereditary positions of high distinction;
yet, in the prime of his youth, he removed his hairpin and left secular life behind.

he subsequently traveled to the capital to seek out and listen to the sūtras and śāstras.
During the Zhenguan era, he studied under Master Xuanzheng at Daxingshan Temple.
Having first studied the Sanskrit language,
he then took up his staff and journeyed westward, fixing his thoughts upon the Jetavana Grove;
turning his back on the golden palace, he departed for the shifting sands.
He traversed the Iron Gate and ascended the Snowy Peaks;
rinsing his mouth at the Fragrant Pond,
he formed his resolve and fully realized the Four Great Vows.
Ascending the Onion Mountains, he raised his heart in a vow to cross over;
traversing the path of the three realms of existence, he swiftly passed through Tukhāra.
Far crossing the lands of the Hu, he arrived at the kingdom of Tibet, where he was escorted northward by Princess Wencheng.
He gradually headed toward the kingdom of Śrāḷandā;
before he had arrived,
he was captured by bandits on a long and perilous road.
Soon thereafter, the merchants' resources were exhausted and they had no one to whom they could appeal;

Perceiving that the bandits were all asleep, he secretly led them out of the encampment;
thus they were spared from the calamity.
He resided in the kingdom of Śrāṅgadhā for four years.
He was honored by the King, who retained him to provide for his needs;
there he studied the Sūtras and Vinaya and practiced the Sanskrit language until he attained some proficiency.
Gradually traveling southward, he reached Mahābodhi and spent another four summer retreats there;

Gazing upon the true image fashioned by Maitreya,

Having resolved his mind upon the Abhidharma and mastered the Vinaya,
he clarified both teachings;

He resided there for three years,
where he studied the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Śata-śāstra*, and other treatises under the Dharma Master Śrīprabha;

The ocean of the Chan gate is vast;

he submitted a memorial reporting [the Master's] true virtues;

He traveled again to the Western Heavens to pursue Xuánzhào back to the capital.
Along the way, at the kingdom of Nīpāla,
he was granted safe passage by the king and escorted to Tufan (Tibet).
He met Princess Wencheng again,
received profound courtesy and hospitality,
and was provided with the means to return to Tang.

Passing through Bālkh, he arrived at Navavihāra—translated into Chinese as "New Monastery"—where he beheld the Tathāgata’s bathing basin and various other sacred sites.
Gradually proceeding to the kingdom of Kāpiśī, he paid homage to the Tathāgata’s cranial bone relic.
Having prepared incense and flowers and taken up the seal-text,
he contemplated the good and evil of his future lives.
Then, crossing the Sindhu River, he finally reached Rāḍha.
Having received the king’s respectful hospitality for four years during the summer retreat,
he traveled southward and gathered various medicinal herbs with the hope of returning to the Eastern Land (China).
He proceeded to the Vajrāsana and circumambulated it.

fulfilling all the aspirations of his life.

He further studied the Vyākaraṇa (grammar), thoroughly mastering its essential principles.
He possessed excellent calligraphic skill in both the regular and cursive scripts.
He erected a stele composed in the Tang style at Dajue Temple and brought with him over four hundred scrolls of new and old Buddhist sūtras and śāstras from the Tang kingdom.
They were both at Nālandā.

while staying in the kingdom of Āmalapadra, he fell ill and passed away.

Suddenly here, he encountered the end of his path.
